name: Mexico
summary_text: Legal gender recognition remains unfinished and uneven across Mexico. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's states now operate administrative procedures for legal gender recognition, and called on the states that lack such procedures to adopt them. The same dispatch warned that implementation differs sharply from one state to another, and that where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.  The barriers are documented concretely. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police. That report set these findings against killings including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.  Formal rights and their enforcement diverge. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog (22 November 2024) found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice. Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.  Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.  Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide. The law is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital.  Regional oversight bodies have pressed the authorities. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.

sources.title: Article 1, Constitution of Mexico amendment prohibiting discrimination
sources.documents: Prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation; inserts precise term 'sexual orientation' into federal constitutional protection.
sources.detail: Cited as amended 2001 with term 'preferences', then June 2011 with 'sexual orientation'

sources.title: Supreme Court nationwide jurisprudence on same-sex adoption / parental rights
sources.documents: Binds all lower court judges to rule in favor of same-sex couples seeking adoption and parental rights; follows Campeche adoption ban case.
sources.detail: Cited as finalized 23 September 2016; related rulings 11 August 2015 and September 2016

name: Marshall Islands
summary_text: The Republic of the Marshall Islands has no criminalisation regime covering consensual same-sex conduct. Human Dignity Trust's record of the global history of criminalisation dates the country's decriminalisation to 2005, so a visitor faces no statutory offence for consensual same-sex relations.  The most recent official country reporting in the inventory is the United States Department of State's 2015 Human Rights Report on the Marshall Islands. It recorded no reports of torture, arbitrary killings, enforced disappearances or LGBT-specific abuses, and it listed prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence among the significant problems it identified.

sources.title: Gender Equality Act 2019
sources.documents: Prohibits direct/indirect discrimination in all areas including on sexual orientation or gender identity; requires government measures to eliminate stereotypes/prejudice and sensitize judicial/law enforcement officials
sources.detail: Cited in article as 'Gender Equality Act 2019'; no URL visible in provided text
